- When sentiment is negative (especially > -0.5) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak values.
- If model shows sharp upward spike in forecast (e.g., >+5% from prior day) and sentiment is neutral or positive, it often overestimates — cap or dampen the spike.
- If recent history shows strong downward trend + negative sentiment, model often underestimates — adjust forecast downward by 1–2% to match mean reversion.
- Model frequently overestimates early in 30-day horizon when sentiment is positive — reduce first 5–7 days’ forecast by 1–3%.
- When sentiment is consistently low (e.g., 3+ consecutive negative values), model tends to underestimate — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to compensate.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome by 2–4% over 5+ days, apply downward bias correction — especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- If sentiment turns positive after a negative period, model often overshoots — reduce forecast by 1–2% in the first 3–5 days of the new sentiment phase.
- Model underestimates when sentiment is weak or flat — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to account for low volatility bias.
- If model forecast is below true outcome by 2–4% over 5+ days, consider upward bias — especially if sentiment is positive or neutral.
